Righteous Anger
rī´chŭs ăng´gẽr
n. phrase (anger aroused by what is genuinely evil, held without sin)
Righteous from Old English rihtwis, right-wise; anger from Old Norse angr, grief or affliction — the Norse root carries sorrow in it, which is exactly what distinguishes the righteous kind from the other.

Biblical Definition

Righteous anger is anger at evil, held without sin. It is permitted and bounded in one verse: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath” (Eph 4:26). The Lord shows it, and its companion emotion is named: He “looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts” (Mar 3:5). He acts on it in the temple, having made “a scourge of small cords” (John 2:15). It is an attribute of God: “God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day” (Psa 7:11). And the standing caution stands beside all of it: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines anger as a violent passion of the mind excited by a real or supposed injury; and notes that anger is not properly a synonym of resentment, being often justifiable when its cause is just and its expression restrained.

expand to see more

ANGER, n. A violent passion of the mind excited by a real or supposed injury; usually accompanied with a propensity to take vengeance, or to obtain satisfaction from the offending party.

Anger is also excited by an injury offered to a relation, friend or party to which one is attached; and some degrees of it may be excited by cruelty, injustice or oppression offered to those with whom one has no immediate connection, or even to the community of which one is a member.

Nor is it unusual to see something of this passion roused by gross absurdities in others, especially in controversy or discussion.

Anger may be inflamed till it rises to rage and a temporary delirium.

Key Scripture

Eph 4:26 — "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:"

Mar 3:5 — "And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other."

John 2:15 — "And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;"

Psa 7:11 — "God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day."

Jas 1:20 — "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God."

Modern Corruption

A man's temper is baptised as righteous anger, and the tests Scripture supplies are all ones it fails.

expand to see more

Mark 3:5 gives the signature and it is two emotions in one look: He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts. Grief is the article that is nearly always missing from the counterfeit. Righteous anger sorrows over the people it is aimed at and would be delighted to be made unnecessary by their repentance; the counterfeit enjoys itself, rehearses the offence, and is faintly disappointed when the offender turns out to have an explanation. That test is available to any man in about thirty seconds and is almost never applied.

The second test is the object. The Lord's recorded anger is provoked by hardness toward the suffering, by obstruction of the weak, by His Father's house made a market — never by an insult to Himself, and when He was reviled He reviled not again. Most anger that presents itself as righteous is aroused most reliably by offences against the angry man's own standing, and that single observation disposes of the majority of cases. Webster is unusually helpful here, allowing that anger may justly be roused by cruelty or oppression offered to strangers, and noting drily that it is also roused by gross absurdities in others, especially in controversy.

The third test is duration, and Ephesians 4:26 supplies it as a hard practical limit that bypasses self-assessment entirely: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Whatever the anger's merits, it has a curfew. Paul adds in the next verse the reason — neither give place to the devil — treating retained anger as an opening rather than a conviction. An indignation that survives the night is being kept, and a man keeping it should ask what for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek orgizo (G3710), to be angry; orge (G3709), settled anger; parorgismos (G3950), provocation, wrath; sullupeomai (G4818), to be grieved with.

expand to see more

Greek orgizesthe kai me hamartanete (G3710) — be ye angry, and sin not; Ephesians 4:26, quoting Psalm 4:4.

Greek met' orges…sullupoumenos (G3709, G4818) — with anger, being grieved; Mark 3:5.

Greek orge anthropou (G3709) — the wrath of man; James 1:20.

Usage

"“With anger, being grieved” — and the grief is what is usually missing."

"“Let not the sun go down upon your wrath” — a curfew, whatever the merits."

"“The wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” — however righteous it feels."
